[sec. 4.1.4 Tone, pp. 58-59] From the study, it has been established that in addition to phonemes contrasting meaning, Mbunda also uses tone to contrast meaning in some words. There are two types of tone in the language under study; high tone and low tone. In the examples below, only high tone is marked: (45) a) aká „put‟ aka „this little thing‟ b) mukánda „puberty camp‟ múkanda „letter‟ c) límo „pregnancy‟ limo „a single big thing‟ d) nána „mother‟ nana „a cheek‟ ... g) mbunda „waist‟ Mbúnda „language (Mbunda language)‟ ... j) vuli „loneliness‟ vulí „which?‟ [Kashoki & Mann 1978, sec. 3.4 Tone and Stress, p. 70, areal:] In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, however, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. ... In any case, independent of the lengthening of vowels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of all Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone.

new_statements.quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, however, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. However, it must be remembered that that is also the syllable, according to the rule mentioned earlier, which is lengthened, so that the stress may be the effect of the lengthening of the vowel. In any case, independent of the lengthening of vowels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of all Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Areal statement for the 25 Zambian languages the authors surveyed (Mbunda included): no contrastive word stress; syllables roughly evenly stressed; where a penult sounds stronger it is a by-product of penultimate vowel lengthening; every syllable carries one of two contrastive tones (H, L). No Mbunda-specific stress rule is given anywhere in the chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: Penult 'slightly greater force' in some languages (Cewa cited) attributed to the penultimate-lengthening rule; that rule (pp. 63-64) is stated for Eastern Province languages and 'several languages of the Northwestern Province' without naming Mbunda.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, impressionistic, generic to 'Zambian languages' as a class; Mbunda is in the sample (Table 2:1) but is not individually discussed under stress or tone. Zambian Mbunda only (Angolan Mbunda not covered).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is areal ('Zambian languages'), from a survey whose 25-language sample includes Mbunda (Table 2:1) but never discusses Mbunda's own stress or tone; it covers Zambian (Western/Northwestern Province) Mbunda only. Angolan Mbunda (Diarra 1985/1990, Luanda ILN) is undescribed here. Glottolog's Figanière 1864 'grammar sketch' for mck is actually about Kimbundu (kimb1241) and should be discounted. No Mbunda-specific stress statement was found in any accessible source; treat the catalog entry as 'tonal, no contrastive word stress per areal survey', low confidence.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tone language with a stress statement reading from Kashoki & Mann 1978: it confirms, for Mbunda specifically, a two-tone lexical contrast (H vs L, minimal pairs) and adds contrastive vowel length, but it deliberately says nothing about stress placement, so the areal 'more or less evenly stressed' statement of Kashoki & Mann remains the only stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is explicitly placed outside the scope of the dissertation; the phonology chapter establishes two contrastive tones (high, low) and contrastive vowel length for Mbunda, with no statement on where stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: The penultimate-lengthening passage (p. 14) is about Cinsenga (Miti 2001) and the penultimate-stress passage (p. 26, 'there is a stress on the last syllable but one (the penult) of each word in Lamba') is about Lamba; neither is a Mbunda statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Figanière 1864 describes 'Bunda's Language, or Angolense' / 'Ambunda' = Kimbundu (H.21, Luanda), not K.15 Mbunda [mck]; the Glottolog/EBALL link to mbun1249 is a name-based misattribution. Kalyata 2020 describes the Zambian dialect Mbunda ya Mathzi (Katavola) of Kalabo and Lukulu Districts, Western Province, and states it does not cover Mbunda as spoken in Angola. Kashoki & Mann 1978 (existing statement) covers Northwestern/Western Province Zambian Mbunda as part of an areal sketch.

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress' p. 70 (areal, for the 25 Zambian languages studied, Mbunda among them per Table 2:1 pp. 28-29): syllables are more or less evenly stressed; in some languages (e.g. Cewa) the penult seems slightly stronger, which may be an effect of penultimate lengthening; stress never distinguishes words; every syllable carries tone, two contrastive tones H/L. Mbunda is named individually only for its th/d fricatives (p. 68); penultimate lengthening (pp. 63-64) is attributed to Eastern Province languages and 'several languages of the Northwestern Province' without naming Mbunda.
